strengths: The paper addresses an important practical weakness of diffusion-based all-in-one image restoration: slow inference. Using VAR-style scale-space autoregression is a timely and plausible direction, and the reported speedup over LDM-based baselines is substantial.

The method is technically coherent, combining degraded-image cross-attention, continuous latent conditioning, a latent refinement transformer, and VAE decoder fine-tuning to adapt a pretrained generative backbone to restoration.

The empirical section covers multiple degradation types and includes full-reference metrics, no-reference real-world/generalization metrics, qualitative examples, runtime comparisons, a user study, and several ablations.

The scale-space analysis of VAR latents is an interesting observation: coarse scales appear to capture degradation while finer scales retain scene details, giving useful motivation for the architecture.
Among the evaluated generative AiOR methods, RestoreVAR consistently improves PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS while being much faster, which is a meaningful result for this sub-area.
weaknesses: The central performance claim is somewhat narrow: RestoreVAR is state of the art mainly among generative AiOR methods, while non-generative methods remain clearly stronger on standard full-reference restoration metrics across several datasets.

The evaluation relies heavily on no-reference metrics and a user study to support generalization and perceptual superiority. MUSIQ/CLIPIQA can favor natural-looking generative outputs without verifying restoration correctness, and the user study lacks detail about protocol, randomization, statistical significance, and participant quality control.

Some baseline choices may bias the comparison. AutoDIR is evaluated without its structure correction module, several baselines use public checkpoints rather than retraining under matched data/resolution settings, and task-specific restoration models are excluded despite being relevant upper bounds for individual degradations.

Ablations are useful but incomplete. The paper does not sufficiently isolate the contribution of cross-attention, RoPE, AdaLN removal, decoder fine-tuning losses, training each component independently, or the amount of pretrained VAR knowledge retained.

The novelty is moderate rather than exceptional: the work is a strong adaptation of VAR/HART-style components to AiOR, but several ingredients are inherited or natural extensions, and the paper could better distinguish what is fundamentally new from engineering integration.

Reproducibility is limited in the main paper. Important architectural details, complexity derivations, limitations, and qualitative results are deferred to supplementary material, and there is no clear statement about code/model release or enough detail to fully reproduce training.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing the high inference cost of diffusion-based all-in-one image restoration while retaining generative priors.

The proposed direction of adapting scale-space visual autoregressive modeling to restoration is potentially interesting, and the paper provides a reasonably clear high-level architecture with conditioning, latent refinement, and decoder fine-tuning.

The reported inference speed is substantially better than the compared latent-diffusion restoration methods, and the paper includes results across several common restoration tasks and degradation types.
The latent refiner ablation suggests that converting discrete VAR latents to continuous latents is important for restoration fidelity.
weaknesses: The main empirical claim is much weaker than stated. RestoreVAR only outperforms the selected generative baselines, while it remains clearly behind many non-generative AiOR methods on standard full-reference metrics. The paper frames this as state-of-the-art restoration too aggressively.

The comparison protocol raises fairness concerns. Some non-generative methods are retrained, while most generative methods use public checkpoints that may not be trained or tuned under comparable data, resolution, task coverage, or inference settings. The AutoDIR structure correction module is removed, which may disadvantage a key baseline.

The novelty is incremental. Cross-attention conditioning, decoder fine-tuning, adversarial/perceptual reconstruction losses, and latent refinement are standard design choices; the paper does not convincingly isolate which aspects are specific to VAR rather than a straightforward adaptation of existing generative restoration recipes.

The ablation study is incomplete for the paper's central claims. There is no sufficiently detailed ablation of cross-attention placement, degraded-latent conditioning strength, RoPE, AdaLN removal, decoder fine-tuning versus refiner contributions, training data scale, or model-size/speed/quality tradeoffs.

The scale-space analysis is visually suggestive but not rigorous. The claim that coarse scales capture degradations and fine scales encode scene details is central to the motivation, yet it is supported mainly by qualitative examples rather than quantitative analysis across degradations and datasets.

The generalization evidence is not very convincing. The paper relies heavily on no-reference IQA metrics such as MUSIQ and CLIPIQA, which are known to be imperfect proxies for restoration correctness and can reward perceptual artifacts or hallucinated detail.

The user study is under-specified: participant instructions, randomization, blinding, statistical significance, variance, and per-criterion scores are not reported, making it difficult to judge the reliability of the claimed human preference advantage.

Reproducibility is limited in the main paper. Many architectural and training details are deferred to the supplementary, and the paper does not clearly specify parameter counts, FLOPs, memory use, sampling settings, exact preprocessing, or whether code/checkpoints will be released.

The method may hallucinate or alter image content, but the paper does not provide a sufficient failure analysis or safety discussion for restoration scenarios where fidelity matters, despite explicitly relying on generative priors.

Overall, the paper has an interesting direction and some promising numbers, but the evidence does not support acceptance at a top-tier AI venue: the contribution is not sufficiently novel, the evaluation is not robust enough, and several central claims are overstated.

strengths: Timely and meaningful contribution: adapting scale-space visual autoregressive modeling to generative all-in-one image restoration is a clear idea with practical relevance, especially given the speed limitations of LDM-based restoration.

The method is technically well motivated, combining degraded-image cross-attention, decoder fine-tuning on continuous latents, and a lightweight latent refinement transformer to address plausible failure modes of directly using VAR for restoration.

Empirical results are strong among generative AiOR methods: RestoreVAR consistently improves PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS over Diff-Plugin, AutoDIR, and PixWizard across five standard degradations, while reporting a large inference-time advantage.
The paper includes useful ablations for continuous vs. discrete conditioning, decoder adversarial fine-tuning, and latent refiner variants, supporting several key design choices.

The evaluation goes beyond synthetic benchmarks by including real-world, unseen, and mixed degradations, plus a small user study, which helps substantiate the claimed perceptual/generalization benefits.
weaknesses: The method remains clearly behind strong non-generative AiOR models on full-reference synthetic benchmarks, often by large PSNR/SSIM margins, so the practical advantage depends heavily on accepting the generative/perceptual framing rather than restoration fidelity alone.

The comparison to generative baselines may not be fully decisive: some baselines use public checkpoints while others are retrained or modified, and AutoDIR is evaluated without its structure correction module. More controlled retraining or standardized inference settings would strengthen the evidence.

The scale-space analysis motivating the method is mostly qualitative. A quantitative analysis showing degradation information concentration across VAR scales would make this central claim more convincing.

Generalization evaluation relies on no-reference metrics such as MUSIQ and CLIPIQA, which are useful but imperfect proxies for restoration correctness and can favor perceptual naturalness over fidelity. More human-study detail, statistical analysis, and failure cases would help.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the main paper: important architectural details, data mixing strategy, exact model sizes, training schedules for all components, and complexity breakdowns are deferred to supplementary material, and code release is not discussed.

The user study is promising but relatively small and under-specified: the paper reports 36 responses over 50 scenes but lacks details on randomization, ranking protocol, inter-rater variability, confidence intervals, and whether raters were blinded.

strengths: The paper proposes a timely and technically plausible adaptation of visual autoregressive modeling to all-in-one image restoration, with a coherent architecture: degraded-image cross-attention, RoPE-based scaling, continuous-latent decoder fine-tuning, and a lightweight latent refiner.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is not fully aligned with several strong claims. RestoreVAR clearly improves over the selected LDM-based baselines on Table 1, but it remains substantially worse than non-generative AiOR methods on standard full-reference metrics, sometimes by large margins. The paper frames this as a generative-model tradeoff, but the main claims should be more carefully scoped.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing the inference cost of generative all-in-one image restoration while retaining perceptual quality.
The proposed system is reasonably well motivated and combines several sensible components: VAR conditioning, cross-attention to degraded-image latents, a latent refiner, and decoder fine-tuning.
The runtime advantage over LDM-based restoration baselines is substantial, and the paper reports detailed compute comparisons, including steps, latency, TFLOPs, and parameter counts.
Ablations support several design choices, especially continuous-latent conditioning and the latent refiner, which appear important for the reported performance.
weaknesses: The main empirical claim is much weaker than presented: RestoreVAR is far below strong non-generative AiOR methods on full-reference metrics in Table 1, so the contribution is mostly limited to outperforming a small set of LDM-based generative baselines that themselves perform poorly on these benchmarks.

The positioning around generative advantages is not convincingly established. The paper claims better generalization and perceptual realism, but relies heavily on no-reference metrics and a small user study rather than rigorous full-reference or task-grounded evaluation on real degradations.

The comparison protocol is questionable. Some methods are retrained, others use public checkpoints, PixWizard is evaluated as-is, and AutoDIR's structure correction module is removed. Even if the authors motivate this choice, it makes the baseline comparison less directly representative of deployed competing systems.

Novelty is limited. The method largely adapts known ideas from VAR/HART-style latent autoregression, conditioning via cross-attention, decoder fine-tuning, and latent refinement to image restoration. The paper does not clearly isolate a deep technical insight beyond engineering these pieces together.

The scale-space analysis is mostly qualitative and does not provide a rigorous quantitative basis for the central claim that degradations are captured primarily in coarse VAR scales across tasks and real-world settings.

Important baselines are missing or underdeveloped, especially VAR-based restoration alternatives such as Varformer in the AiOR setting, stronger diffusion acceleration/distillation baselines, and task-specific restoration models for context.

The user study methodology is weakly described: participants appear to evaluate outputs via numbered folders/links, and it is unclear whether ordering, method identity, image selection, and repeated-measure effects were properly controlled.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: code is only promised after review, and several implementation details and training choices appear empirically tuned without enough information to independently reproduce the results.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and timely contribution: adapting visual autoregressive modeling to generative all-in-one image restoration, targeting a real limitation of latent diffusion restoration methods, namely slow inference.

The proposed design is technically sensible and well motivated. Cross-attention conditioning on degraded-image latents, RoPE for resolution scaling, decoder fine-tuning, and the latent refinement transformer form a coherent system rather than a superficial application of VAR.

The empirical results are strong against LDM-based generative AiOR baselines: RestoreVAR improves PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS across the main synthetic restoration benchmarks while being much faster, with detailed runtime, TFLOP, and parameter comparisons.

The paper includes useful ablations for continuous versus discrete conditioning, latent refiner variants, VAE decoder losses, positional embeddings, and scale-space behavior, which support several of the architectural choices.

The evaluation is broad, spanning dehazing, desnowing, deraining, low-light enhancement, deblurring, real-world/unseen/mixed degradations, qualitative comparisons, and a user study with statistical analysis in the supplement.
The writing is generally clear, and the paper articulates a plausible reason why VAR's coarse-to-fine latent structure is suitable for image restoration.
weaknesses: The main quantitative advantage is largely over other generative methods; standard non-generative AiOR methods remain substantially better on in-distribution pixel-level metrics in Table 1, so the claimed closing of the fidelity gap should be stated more cautiously.

The generalization claims rely heavily on no-reference metrics such as MUSIQ and CLIPIQA plus a user study. These are useful but not fully decisive, and Table 2 shows RestoreVAR is competitive but not clearly best among generative methods on average.

The comparison to AutoDIR is debatable because the paper removes AutoDIR's structure correction module. The supplementary argues this is fair for isolating generative behavior, but from an end-user restoration perspective this excludes part of a competing system.

Novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental: the work combines a pretrained VAR backbone with conditioning and latent refinement components that are conceptually close to existing generative restoration and HART-style refinement ideas.

The paper would benefit from stronger evidence on hallucination risk and semantic faithfulness, especially because generative restoration can invent details; the current qualitative examples and user preferences do not fully address this concern.

Reproducibility is only moderate: many training details are given, but the review copy does not make clear whether code, trained checkpoints, exact evaluation scripts, and baseline retraining protocols will be released.
